articles.sourceTitle: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
articles.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
articles.text: All AI-generated code should be Open SourceJakub T. JankiewiczThis may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.

articles.sourceTitle: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals
articles.title: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals, report claims
articles.text:
Connecting the dots: The AI boom has been widely blamed for GPU prices spinning out of control over the past year. Following Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia,new information suggests that this was the goal of the former CEO's business strategy, which has long drawn accusations of circular financing.

A recent Wall Street Journal profile of Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress has shed more light on how Nvidia controversially financed its own customers to drive the AI boom. According to the report, the company pushed for more deals in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb an oversupply of TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high.
Since at least last year, Nvidia has been accused of prolonging the AI boom by supporting the companies that buy its chips. Co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, along with CFO Kress, even went so far as to defend the company against comparisons to Enron, which used similar tactics to illegally obscure its debt before its 2001 collapse.
Also read: GPU Prices Are Spiraling Out of Control - Q4 2026 Update

Behind the scenes, Kress expressed concern about the scale of the deals Nvidia had inked with cloud providers and major AI companies like OpenAI. Nvidia pushed ahead anyway, but by summer 2026, the company was wondering whether it had pushed too far amid an "avalanche" of semiconductors it had ordered from TSMC.
It was around this time that Huang berated Kress, calling her "a deer in headlights," according to someone familiar with the matter. Nvidia began to slow down, downsize, and pause some of its financing deals, including one with OpenAI that originally included a $250 billion backstop for the world's largest data center.

AI data centers have siphoned off DRAM and NAND manufacturing capacity traditionally used for RAM and storage in consumer devices, inflating prices. Nvidia's GeForce GPUs have been hit especially hard, with prices often exceeding 160% of their original MSRP. The company's flagship RTX 5090 has become unobtainable because Nvidia has directed its VRAM and semiconductors toward data center GPUs.
As its financial support deals wound down, Huang became worried about the company's stock market valuation, with its average monthly stock multiple falling far behind those of other large tech companies.
Related: Without Jensen Huang, is it game over for GeForce?

Colette Kress, Interim CEO and Executive VP and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) of Nvidia.
At a Berlin conference, the former CEO told major clients a story about a busy Japanese soup vendor who refused to give him a second serving after he had waited in a long line, saying the vendor had too many customers and not enough soup. Huang used the story to highlight the value of maintaining a diverse customer base and keeping prices high, suggesting that Nvidia's circular financing strategy inflated GPU prices by creating the perception of high demand.
The story emerged after Huang's resignation following the revelation of multiple extramarital affairs. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), whose company, Megaspeed, was suspected by US intelligence of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of export regulations. While some allege that she is a spy for Beijing, President Trump and the Justice Department said that hasn't been determined.

articles.sourceTitle: Jensen Huang allegedly manufactured the GPU shortage
articles.title: Instead Of Lowering GPU Prices, Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Financed AI Startups To Absorb Excess Silicon, Shattering The Shortage Perception
articles.text:
0-20%: Unlikely - Lacks credible sources
21-40%: Questionable - Some concerns remain
41-60%: Plausible - Reasonable evidence
61-80%: Probable - Strong evidence
81-100%: Highly Likely - Multiple reliable sources

Now that NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang is no longer the company CEO, we have some truth behind the exponential rise of semiconductor and memory prices. According to the latest findings, it appears that we were led to believe that there was an organic supply shortage, but in reality, we learn that Jensen was actually leveraging NVIDIA’s own balance sheet to finance AI startups and datacenter buildouts so they could absorb the company’s over-ordered semiconductor shipments from TSMC.

NVIDIA faced an “avalanche” of excess TSMC silicon and memory, and the only way to curb the oversupply was to fund AI startups

The fresh revelations stem from a tense August 2026 confrontation between Huang and NVIDIA’s longtime Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, now the interim CEO. Seeing as how the former head honcho was escalating the GPU maker’s financial exposure, Kress pushed to rein in the company’s “circular financing” commitments to smaller cloud providers and major AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Initial discussions had floated underwriting roughly 8 gigawatts of OpenAI compute valued at up to $250 billion, and Kress successfully scaled NVIDIA’s signed guarantee cap down to roughly 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion. As a result, Jensen reportedly belittled Kress for questioning the deals, referring to her as “a deer in the headlights.”

To justify NVIDIA's need to financially underwrite OpenAI and smaller cloud operators to keep them purchasing its GPUs, Huang privately admitted that major cloud giants were pivoting away from NVIDIA in favor of in-house custom chips. With hyperscalers actively reducing their reliance on “off-the-shelf parts,” Huang acknowledged that the massive volume of prepaid TSMC wafers and memory NVIDIA had committed to buying was “coming at him like an avalanche.”

By funding datacenter expansion for AI startups, NVIDIA effectively created artificial demand to clear out its own surplus silicon instead of letting the supply flood the market and force GPU prices down. Those internal pressures align with earlier assessments from industry analyst Ed Zitron, who estimated that at least $200 billion worth of NVIDIA AI GPUs are sitting idle in warehouses after being purchased by cloud giants that lacked either the electrical grid capacity or immediate end-user demand to power them on. Amazon faced a similar dilemma.

Knowing that the imminent avalanche would be upon NVIDIA sooner rather than later, the company reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down its upcoming chip orders. For PC builders and hardware enthusiasts who have endured years of steep GPU and RAM pricing under the impression of severe component scarcity, the disclosures shatter the shortage narrative and expose the aggressive financial maneuvering used to keep hardware prices elevated.

While Jensen can’t be faulted for making these moves because he was keeping the best interests of the company in mind, it’s a stab in the back for gamers and hardware owners who are unable to locate any mouth-watering deals for GPUs or memory because of the perceived shortage.

News Source: The Wall Street Journal

About the author:  Omar Sohail is a reporter and analyst for Wccftech's mobile section, specializing in the technology and business of the mobile industry. His expertise lies in the intricate hardware supply chain, covering developments in semiconductor manufacturing, chip lithography, and camera sensor technology.

Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title: The Claude Delusion
articles.text:
November 13th, 2026

Something weird happens to people who are successful.
They start to think they're gods.

Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict
pre-requisite of success.  And maybe it's not so much
"being successful", but rather "being rich".  How do
you become rich?  Some people are just lucky.  Lucky
to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able
and willing to nurture your talent, and of course
quite often lucky to have been at
the right place at the right time1.

Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also
work hard.  But even—especially!—the Paris
Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood
superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires
with "a
small loan" (or a share of an emerald mine) from
their fathers—they all
strongly believe that they deserve their
success and then conclude that anybody not as
successful only has themselves to blame.

This is especially the case for people in tech, where
for years and years being good at programming has been
equated with overall (and often: superior)
intelligence2, and those
illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant
Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn "I am good at
writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be
successful" into a train of thought that goes
more like "I am successful. Success is not random,
so I must deserve my success.  I appear to be a
genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is
trivial.  Ergo, I am good at everything."

Bill Gates, MD / PhD Biology

Let's take Bill Gates as an example.
Now, mind you,
Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his
skillset and professional background includes without
a doubt a lot of computer programming and various
ruthless monopolistic business tactics.  In a
recent New York Times interview, he describes how
he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress
(emphasis mine):

And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis
to see the work they were doing, and I challenged
them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook
and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a
perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have
proven that you are reading. That is, encoding
knowledge in an accessible form.

And so it’s six months before the public release that
Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to
my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P.
exam, even on questions that I had made up that it
couldn't possibly have seen — very complex biology
problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No.1.

Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology
and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda
Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles
and research in this field.  But the hubris to think
himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced,
novel questions in a scientific field outside
his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities
and then being "shocked" that it could
answer these questions makes my point.

Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI
can do what he used to do: write code.

And then late last year, when Anthropic's Claude
coding models got super good, I could see that they
are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most
developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13
to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or
better than anyone.

That’s another moment where I went: This is
incredible. That the capability of doing long-running,
complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they
are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in
code.

Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion
that something else could be "as good as I
am" is, first of all, hard to believe and
secondly necessarily means that it's
"superhuman".  That man is not lacking
self-esteem, no sirree, Bob.

Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros
appear to be losing their
minds, and this thinking ("Anything approaching my
skill level is superhuman.") explains a lot about how
we ended up with both stories of ultimate doom and
human extinction as well as the utopian nirvana where
AI solves all of mankind's problems (well, all of the
billionaires' problems, which appear to
largely converge on pesky
mortality).

Revenge of the Nerds

For most tech nerds, being good at programming
computers was a differentiating skill.  It was weird,
normies didn't understand it at all, you spoke your
own language (languages!), you could make a computer
do things.  You understood how the internet
works, and anything that's not working was clearly
written by complete and utter morons, and you could
easily write this yourself in an afternoon if you
wanted to.

So now you've created a computer program that can do
the same thing.  Your mind boggles!  And it speaks!
It confirms you, it praises you, it tells you that
you're brilliant—clearly evidence that it is
infallible itself.  But now imagine if it was
better than you.  What at first seems
inconceivable then must strike fear and awe in your
heart, for you have created a powerful
monster with direction and purpose all its own.
(And you sure have consumed enough pulpy science
fiction to know that your creature is coming for you
eventually.)

"Can you imagine a Beowulf cluster of these?" was an
old Slashdot meme before memes were a thing.
But the notion of having an army of minions to do your
bidding has always appealed to the nerds looking to
assert their superiority, and thus we arrived at
"agents".  "Swarms" of "autonomous" "agents".

This narrative of agency conveniently also relieves
you of responsibility.  You didn't fail to properly
restrict a potentially malicious program you trained
to hack other systems with persistence.  No, the
"agents" went "rogue". You have summoned powerful
daemons indeed.  Daemons that can produce code faster
than you (gasp!), code you don't fully understand
(although of course you could, you just don't want to,
you don't have time, you have too much going on, what
with your homegrown heavily customized harness).
It becomes obvious quite quickly that this, then,
must be SUPERINTELLIGENCE.
Superintelligence that COULD KILL US ALL!

Finally got my agent harness set up just the way I like it.

Power corrupts etc.

I picked on Bill Gates above to illustrate the overconfidence
effect, but of course there is no shortage of much
more exaggerated
egos making bold statements
outside of (or even within)
their purported area of expertise, reflecting a
complete and utter inability to relate to other
people.  Gwyneth Paltrow giving health advice, Richard
Branson trying to compete with Coca-Cola, dozens of
actors trying to become politicians, Fox News anchors
and reality TV stars being given cabinet
positions, Mark Zuckerberg
thinking of running for president, various tech
businesses trying to "disrupt" health care, Elon
Musk's many, many flops, or any of the Elizabeth Holmes
or Sam Bankman-Frieds the industry has no shortage
of...  To them, we're all just NPCs.

The fact that the self-delusional mindset I note here
can then quickly lead to simple, flat out fraud is not
coincidental.  The more powerful people are, the less
empathy they exhibit.  This is neither
news nor limited to tech; dog knows there are
countless rich assholes outside of tech doing
asshole things.  But few outside the tech sector
suffer the same level of delusion, of
thinking themselves solely and uniquely qualified to
decide mankind's future, to claim to have birthed a
digital Prometheus, to boldly declare (and use as a
perpetual shield) a literal Deus ex Machina
to cure
all diseases—if only they could find the
time to prioritize that sort of work over, say, their
military
contracts.

Pretending to even remotely care about climate change3
while at the same time undoing "15
years' worth of greenhouse gas reductions" and then
listing
environmental concerns as a risk factor in your S1
is just the cherry on top.

If these are the new American Gods... well, je
n'ai jamais eu besoin de cette
hypothèse-là.

November 13th, 2026

P.S.: On 2026-11-14, this post was briefly top on
HackerNews, and before being flagged (??) garnered
almost 200
comments.  The majority of that discussion veered
into whether or not Bill Gates is a good programmer,
which really is rather besides the point here.

Footnotes:

[1] The actual citation for "Bill
Gates went to one of the only high schools in the
world that had a computer" is "The
Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel;
Malcolm Gladwell discusses this in Outliers
as well.
↩

[2] The entire interview circus in the tech
world revolved around this notion of exclusivity
and brilliant jerks: "Google hires geniuses"
was an oft-repeated mantra in Silicon Valley, so
logically, if you were hired by Google, you were a genius.
(Yes, all >180,000 of Google's employees.)
This translates to the other big or
exclusive companies, and explains why
everybody leaving will always note
that they were always surrounded by the most
brilliant minds.
It's Inverse Groucho Marx Bias.
↩

[3] And hey, we really don't need AI to "figure out
how to combat climate change".  We already know how to
do it.  We just have to actually show any willingness
to stop it.  Unfortunately, that's also exactly where
these megalomaniacs get in the way.
↩

Links:

Discussion on HackerNews
Everybody's Lost Their Minds
"Winning AI"

articles.sourceTitle: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
articles.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
articles.text: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery.But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will coverdifferent positional methods in LLMs;(finally) how RoPE works;what methods are used by recent open LLMs.Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures.Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here, which also has a navigation bar on the left side.Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.)A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:“The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”“The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps.For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence.(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub.)Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information.The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.Figure 5: GPT-2 adds absolute position information before the transformer blocks, as highlighted in purple. The dimensions shown are for GPT-2 XL.The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and xm the token ID at that position. The input to the first block isHere,Etoken is the embedding layer,Pm is the position info vector selected by m,and hm is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.Figure 6: Token and position embeddings are added element-wise. (I am following the convention here that neural network diagrams are usually read from bottom to top.)In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3]. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding Pm depends on the token’s own position m. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P2 and P7, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)Figure 7: Sinusoidal position encodings added to the token embeddings as highlighted in purple.The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √(dmodel) before adding the position vectors, where dmodel is the embedding width.So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formulathe formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is:This scaling by √(dmodel) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical scales at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them. In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same scale
